verdict.summary: A working dev OAuth client takes under an hour, but most Gmail-agent use cases (read, modify, draft) need restricted scopes, which require verification plus an annual third-party CASA security assessment. Sensitive-only apps (gmail.send, Calendar) need a review of days to weeks, and non-sensitive-only apps can go live the same day.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Self-serve: create project, enable API, fill Branding/Audience/Data Access, create client. Testing mode works immediately for up to 100 listed test users. No review needed.

timeToProd.assumes: Restricted Gmail scopes (read, modify, drafts), which most email agents need.
timeToProd.waitingOn: Google Trust & Safety review (brand, then data access), plus a CASA-authorized security lab's Letter of Validation for restricted scopes

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Google's FAQ estimates brand 2-3 business days, sensitive 10 business days, restricted 6 weeks, 'not guaranteed'. The developer docs say sensitive 'typically 3-5 business days' and restricted 'several weeks'. The upper bounds come from forum reports of reviews stalled for months and the time a CASA lab takes to remediate and retest.

verdict.cost: Google charges no fees. Restricted scopes need an annual CASA assessment paid directly to an authorized lab, roughly US$500-$6,000+/yr per app depending on lab and tier (third-party pricing, unverified). You also need a domain and a hosted homepage and privacy policy.

prerequisites.item: Google account, ideally a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity organization
prerequisites.why: Any Google account can create a Cloud project. An organization is required for the Internal user type and makes project ownership survive staff changes.

prerequisites.item: A domain you own, verified in Google Search Console by a project Owner/Editor
prerequisites.why: All authorized domains must be verified for brand verification. The homepage and privacy policy must live on this domain.

prerequisites.item: Public homepage (not just a login page) linking to a privacy policy on the same domain
prerequisites.why: Brand verification checks the homepage and privacy policy. The privacy policy URL must match the one configured on the Branding page.

prerequisites.item: Privacy policy that discloses Google user data access, use, storage and sharing, plus the Limited Use statement
prerequisites.why: Required by the API Services User Data Policy. Workspace scopes (Gmail/Drive/Calendar) require disclosing adherence to the Limited Use requirements.

prerequisites.item: Support email (a Google account or a Google Group you manage) and developer contact emails that are actually monitored
prerequisites.why: Shown on the consent screen. Trust & Safety sends review requests here, and missed emails stall or fail verification.

prerequisites.item: Separate Cloud projects for dev/staging and production
prerequisites.why: Google recommends separate projects. The unverified user cap is lifetime per project and cannot be reset.

scopeTiers.impact: No verification. In Testing mode these scopes skip the test-user list and the 7-day token expiry. Brand verification is optional, needed only to show your name and logo.
Can publish to production with no scope review. drive.file (per-file access to files the user picks or your app creates) is the main way to avoid restricted Drive scopes.

Requires sensitive scope verification: brand verification, per-scope justification, and an unlisted YouTube demo video. No security assessment. Unverified apps show the 'unverified app' screen and are capped at 100 new users for the project's lifetime.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Gmail and Drive classifications come from Google's scope tables. Calendar: Google cites reading Calendar events as a sensitive-scope example. The Calendar docs have no per-scope sensitivity table, and no Calendar scope appears on any restricted list (inferred).

scopeTiers.impact: Requires restricted scope verification plus an annual CASA security assessment by a Google-approved third-party lab, if restricted data is stored on or passes through your servers. The app must fit an allowed Gmail use case, and Limited Use plus the AI/ML training ban apply. gmail.compose (drafts) is restricted, so an agent that only drafts still needs CASA.

steps.title: Pick the narrowest scopes and map them to tiers
steps.detail: List every feature, then pick the least-privileged scope for each, for example gmail.send instead of gmail.modify, or drive.file instead of drive. Check each scope against Gmail's allowed application types. Whether any restricted scope remains decides whether you face a 1-2 week review or a 2-4 month review with CASA.

steps.title: Create a Google Cloud project (separate dev and prod projects)
steps.detail: Sign in and create a project, ideally under your Workspace/Cloud Identity organization. Create a separate project for production so dev experiments don't burn the prod project's lifetime unverified-user cap.

steps.title: Enable the Gmail / Calendar / Drive APIs
steps.detail: In the API Library, enable gmail.googleapis.com and, if needed, calendar-json.googleapis.com and drive.googleapis.com for the project.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Standard Cloud Console flow. Not quoted from a fetched doc in this research.

steps.title: Configure Google Auth Platform > Branding
steps.detail: Set the app name (must not imply Google or other brands), user support email, logo (120x120, at most 1MB), homepage, privacy policy and ToS URLs, authorized domains, and developer contacts. Add authorized domains before redirect URIs. An agent can draft all the text, but a human must enter it.

steps.title: Configure Google Auth Platform > Audience (user type, test users)
steps.detail: Choose External (any Google account) or Internal (only your org, no verification needed). For External apps, publishing status starts as Testing. Add up to 100 test users. Their authorizations and refresh tokens expire 7 days after consent unless you request only basic profile scopes.

steps.title: Declare scopes in Google Auth Platform > Data Access
steps.detail: Add every scope the app requests. The console groups them as non-sensitive, sensitive, or restricted. Requesting an undeclared scope at runtime can trigger verification problems.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The URL path /auth/scopes for the Data Access page is inferred from a login redirect, not seen rendered.

steps.title: Create an OAuth client (Web application) and set redirect URIs
steps.detail: Create a Web application client, add your exact callback URLs, and store the client ID and secret in your secret manager. Use access_type=offline (plus prompt=consent on first connect) to get a refresh token. Endpoints are listed in the OIDC discovery doc.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Endpoints confirmed live via discovery doc. The client-creation UI was not observed.

steps.title: Build and test the OAuth flow with test users
steps.detail: Implement the auth-code flow with PKCE (S256 supported), token refresh, revocation handling, and invalid_grant recovery. Test with listed test users. Expect a 7-day token expiry in Testing mode, so don't mistake it for a bug.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: Fetched the discovery doc on 2026-10-19: auth https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth, token https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token, revoke https://oauth2.googleapis.com/revoke, PKCE plain/S256.

steps.title: Verify domain ownership in Google Search Console
steps.detail: Verify every authorized domain in Search Console using a Google account that is an Owner or Editor on the Cloud project. Usually a DNS TXT record. An agent can add the record if it has DNS access.

steps.title: Draft privacy policy, homepage copy, and Limited Use disclosure
steps.detail: The privacy policy must explain exactly which Google data is accessed and how it is used, stored, shared, and deleted. Include the statement that use of information from Google Workspace APIs adheres to the Google API Services User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements. If you use AI, say Google data is not used to train generalized models. Host it on the verified domain and link it from the homepage.

steps.title: Publish app (Testing -> In production) and verify branding
steps.detail: On Audience, click Publish app. On Branding, click Verify Branding. The automated check usually finishes in minutes, and manual review takes about 2-3 business days. A compliant result must be published within 7 days or the status becomes 'Need to re-verify'. Published branding is required before you can request data access verification.

steps.title: Write scope justifications and script the demo video
steps.detail: For each sensitive or restricted scope, explain the user-facing feature and why a narrower scope won't work. Write a demo script showing the app name, the full English consent screen with the exact scopes, and each scope being used in the product.

steps.title: Record the demo video and upload it to YouTube as Unlisted
steps.detail: Screen-record the end-to-end flow on the production app, with the same name and branding as submitted. Upload it to YouTube Studio with visibility set to Unlisted.

steps.title: Submit for data access verification (Verification Center)
steps.detail: From Verification Center, prepare and submit justifications, the video link, and confirmations. Then watch the developer contact inbox, because Trust & Safety follow-up emails drive the timeline.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The /auth/verification URL is inferred from a login redirect, not seen rendered.

steps.title: Wait for sensitive/restricted scope review
steps.detail: Google estimates 10 business days for sensitive scopes (the dev docs say 3-5) and 6 weeks for restricted, 'not guaranteed' and dependent on how fast you respond. Reply to every Trust & Safety email quickly, since each round trip resets your place.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Sources conflict on the sensitive timeline (3-5 vs 10 business days). Forum reports describe months-long stalls.

steps.title: Restricted only: complete the CASA security assessment
steps.detail: Once Google says it's time, engage a CASA-authorized lab. Google assigns the assurance level (AL1/AL2, historically called Tier 2/Tier 3). Remediate findings, then the lab sends a Letter of Validation to Google. You pay the lab directly, and Google charges nothing. Tier 3/AL2 needs read-only cloud access for the assessor.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Duration comes from third-party lab marketing, not Google.

steps.title: Wait for final approval; calendar annual re-verification
steps.detail: After approval, the unverified screen and the 100-user cap are removed. Restricted-scope apps must be reassessed at least every 12 months from the LOA date. Changing the name, logo, URLs, or scopes triggers re-verification.

agentCanDo: Map features to the narrowest Gmail/Calendar/Drive scopes and flag which ones are restricted
Draft the privacy policy, ToS, homepage copy, and the Limited Use disclosure
Write per-scope justifications and a shot-by-shot demo video script
Generate the OAuth client config, redirect URIs, and PKCE/refresh/revocation code
Check the live OIDC discovery doc and test token refresh and invalid_grant handling

humanMustDo: Sign in to Google Cloud Console and create the projects
Fill in Branding, Audience, Data Access and OAuth clients (console clicks)
Verify domain ownership in Search Console as a project Owner/Editor
Click Publish app, Verify Branding and Submit for verification
Record and upload the demo video (unlisted YouTube)
Monitor the developer contact inbox and respond to Trust & Safety
Choose, contract and pay a CASA lab, and grant it access
Attest to policy compliance and own annual re-verification

blockers.symptom: "Access blocked: <app> has not completed the Google verification process" / Error 403: access_denied
blockers.cause: The app is in Testing and the signing-in account is not on the test-user list, or the app requests unverified scopes
blockers.fix: Add the account under Audience > Test users, or publish and complete verification for those scopes

evidence.label: unverified
evidence.note: Error text comes from community threads. The mechanism (Testing = test users only) is sourced in s1.

blockers.symptom: Refresh token stops working after ~7 days: invalid_grant "Token has been expired or revoked"
blockers.cause: External app in Testing status requesting more than basic profile scopes, so tokens expire 7 days after consent
blockers.fix: Publish to In production (and verify if needed). Re-consent test users in the meantime.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The exact invalid_grant message wording is not quoted in the sources.

blockers.symptom: "Google hasn't verified this app" warning before the consent screen
blockers.cause: Published app requests sensitive/restricted scopes that are not yet approved
blockers.fix: Submit for verification. Users can click through during the interim, but only 100 new users ever.

blockers.symptom: New users can't connect: OAuth user cap reached
blockers.cause: An unverified app hits the 100-new-user lifetime cap, which cannot be reset
blockers.fix: Complete verification. Use a fresh prod project rather than one used for experiments.

blockers.symptom: Old refresh tokens silently stop working
blockers.cause: Google keeps 100 refresh tokens per account per client ID, and issuing a new one invalidates the oldest
blockers.fix: Reuse stored refresh tokens. Don't force prompt=consent on every login.

blockers.symptom: Verification stuck 'In review' for weeks or months with no Trust & Safety email
blockers.cause: Review queue backlog, or an email sent to an unmonitored developer contact address
blockers.fix: Check that contact addresses are monitored, check spam, and reply promptly. There is no paid expedite.

evidence.label: unverified
evidence.note: Single forum report (Apr-Aug 2026 pending), no Google resolution.

blockers.symptom: Workspace users see 'app blocked' / need admin approval
blockers.cause: The customer's Workspace admin restricts unconfigured third-party apps via API controls
blockers.fix: Ask the customer's admin to mark your OAuth client ID as Trusted in Admin console > Security > API controls

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The help page says access is 'blocked by default' for unconfigured apps. It is unclear whether this applies to all tenants or only those with restrictive settings.

blockers.symptom: Brand verification status reverts to 'Need to re-verify'
blockers.cause: The compliant result was not published within 7 days, or the name/logo/URLs were edited
blockers.fix: Publish branding promptly after the result. Avoid branding edits during review.

blockers.cause: Requested broader scopes than features need (e.g. mail.google.com for read-only)
blockers.fix: Downscope and justify why narrower scopes won't work, for each scope

nuances.text: Internal user type (Workspace/Cloud Identity org only) skips verification entirely and avoids CASA. This is a good fit for agents deployed to a single company, but useless for consumer Gmail users.
Gmail drafting (gmail.compose) and reading (gmail.readonly/metadata) are restricted, while gmail.send is only sensitive. A send-only agent avoids CASA.

AI agents: Workspace data may not be used to create, train, or improve ML/AI models beyond that user's personalized model. Gmail policy (updated 2026-09-03) explicitly allows generative AI summaries and requires restricted-scope apps to protect against prompt injection (Model Armor or equivalent).

Gmail restricted scopes are allowed only for specific app types: email clients, backup, productivity (CRM, mail merge, gen-AI summaries), and reporting/monitoring. One-time export tools and mobile keyboards are prohibited.

CASA is needed only if restricted data is stored on or transmitted through your servers, according to the restricted scope verification page. Purely client-side apps may avoid it, but agents almost always process server-side.
Google's FAQ mentions a 'free tier 2 assessment' path (self-scan) versus paying a lab. Current ADA docs describe both AL1 and AL2 as lab-verified. Expect to pay a lab.

evidence.label: unverified
evidence.note: Sources conflict. Third-party prices: TAC ~$540-$720 Tier 2, Tier 3 ~$3.6k-$4.5k+; Leviathan $3k-$6k Tier 2.

nuances.text: Testing exception: if you request only openid/email/profile, test users don't need to be listed and tokens don't expire after 7 days.
Under 100 users ('personal use') can technically run unverified in production, with users clicking through the warning, but the cap is lifetime per project.
Unified API vendors (e.g. Nylas shared app) let you skip verification and CASA by using their pre-verified project, at the cost of their name on the consent screen and vendor lock-in.
